name: TrendFromOpen

name: PriorSessionHighLowOpenCloseMagnet

name: MiddleOfDayMiddleOfRangeCautionFilter
quote: The middle third of the day, from around 8:30 a.m. until 10:30 a.m. PST, can be difficult for traders on days that are not clearly trending... If the market is trading in the approximate middle of the day's range... and it is now in the middle of the day's trading hours, the chance of a tight trading range with overlapping bars, big tails, and multiple small reversals is significant.
description: During the middle third of the trading session (the book's example: 8:30-10:30 a.m. PST) while price sits near the middle of the day's range, expect choppy, low-quality price action; avoid anything less than a very good entry and prefer waiting for a test of the day's high or low.
book_order_type: n/a (context filter that raises the entry-quality bar rather than blocking entries outright)

complexity.reason: a time-of-day window test plus the day's running high/low and a proximity-to-midpoint test, each simple, combined into one filter

notes: The book explicitly frames the time window as a guideline, not a hard rule ("the time parameters are only guidelines... the overriding factor is the price action") -- see Figure PIV.4 discussion, page 142.

name: SessionAverageBarRangeMoneyStop
quote: Some traders would have used a money stop, like around the height of an average bar so far today, maybe 10 to 15 cents.
description: Size the protective stop as a multiple of the average bar range observed so far in the current session, rather than a fixed dollar amount or a rolling multi-day ATR.
book_order_type: protective stop order at entry price minus the sized distance

complexity.reason: needs a session-relative running average of bar range that resets at each new session, distinct from the corpus's rolling multi-bar ATR

notes: Distinct from AtrTrailingStop/AtrBandBreakout because the averaging window is 'so far today' (session-relative and growing), not a fixed rolling N-bar window.

name: StopBeyondAverageDailyRangeFraction
quote: Some traders will consider that the trend is still in effect unless the market falls more than between 50 to 75 percent of the average daily range.
description: Use a money-management stop sized as a fraction of the instrument's average daily range, rather than a fixed tick count or the signal-bar extreme.
book_order_type: money-management stop sized as a fraction of the average daily range

complexity.reason: needs a design decision on computing a session/daily range aggregate from the strategy's own bar series, which the engine does not currently expose

name: AdaptiveStopFloorFromFirstTradeMAE
quote: After the market turned down on bar 2, they could have calculated that the market went eight ticks against them before it went their way. That meant that the minimum initial protective stop that they would have had to use to stay in the trade was nine ticks, and they would have remembered that for the rest of the day.
description: Use the maximum adverse excursion of the session's first trade (the number of ticks the market moved against the position before turning) as a floor on the stop size for all subsequent trades that session.
book_order_type: money-management stop no smaller than the day's first trade's maximum adverse excursion plus one tick

complexity.reason: requires tracking and persisting a per-session statistic (the first trade's MAE) across subsequent, independent trades -- a session-state design decision the engine does not currently expose

name: AvoidScalingInLastHourOfDay

description: Strength or weakness in the final closingWindowMinutes of today's session biases the odds for tomorrow's/the next higher-timeframe bar's trend direction; usable as a next-session context filter.

name: FirstHourFavorableEntryWindow
quote: There is a tendency for the first hour or two to be the most likely time of the day to find a trade where you can make two to three times your risk... most traders should work very hard to take trades in the first hour or two.
description: Restrict or favor entries to the first N hours of the trading session (the exchange clock's close time), when the reward:risk:probability combination is best.
pseudocode: ctx.Time() >= sessionOpenTime && ctx.Time() <= sessionOpenTime + firstHourMinutes
book_order_type: n/a (context filter, not itself an order)

complexity.reason: a fixed clock-time window test, same shape as the existing TimeWindow rule

name: FinalHourTrendContinuationNoPullbackEntry
quote: Traders who want to enter on pullbacks get trapped out because a pullback never comes. If you see this, enter with the trend on the close of the current bar and put your protective stop beyond the other end of the bar.
description: In the final 30-60 minutes of the session, when a strong trend keeps making new closes in the trend direction without a pullback, enter with the trend at the close of the current bar (rather than waiting for a pullback), stop beyond the bar's opposite extreme.
pseudocode: ctx.Time() >= finalPeriodStart && close[0] > close[1] && close[1] > close[2]
book_order_type: buy/sell at the close of the current bar (market), protective stop beyond the low/high of that same bar

complexity.reason: combines a fixed time window with a short run of consecutive same-direction closes as the 'no pullback' momentum test

notes: finalPeriodStart illustrated at 12:30 PST (final 30-60 minutes before the Emini's 1:00 p.m. PST close); the 'no pullback' test (two consecutive same-direction closes) is a reading, Brooks gives no precise count.

name: DailyTrendBiasFinalHourContinuation
quote: When there is a bull trend on the daily chart, there will almost always be more bull trend bars than bear trend bars... experienced traders will be quick to short any rally that begins to reverse down toward the end of the day [of a bear-trend day], expecting a close near the low of the day.
description: In the final 30-60 minutes, bias with-trend entries toward the prevailing daily-chart trend direction (buy pullbacks in a daily bull trend / sell rallies in a daily bear trend), expecting the day to close near its high/low.
pseudocode: dailyBullTrendContext && ctx.Time() >= finalPeriodStart && low[0] > low[1]
book_order_type: n/a (context filter biasing which with-trend entries to take)

complexity.reason: requires a higher-timeframe (daily) trend-context read alongside the intraday final-hour time window

name: PremarketExtremeTestTarget
quote: The premarket extremes are often targets that get tested during the day session.

premarketHigh = highest(high, sessionBars) // computed only over bars where ctx.Time() is within the premarket window, then held constant through the day session
close[0] <= premarketHigh + toleranceTicks * tickSize && close[0] >= premarketHigh - toleranceTicks * tickSize
book_order_type: n/a (a target/context level, not itself a specific order)

quote: Bar 1 on both the Globex chart on the left and on the day session chart on the right is the 6:35 a.m. PST bar.

name: ReversalOffYesterdayCloseTest
quote: Bar 1 was a sharp pullback to test yesterday's strong close, and it quickly reversed up, creating a buy entry at one tick above the high of the bar 1 pullback.
description: Early in the session, price pulls back to touch (or come within a tick range of) yesterday's close and reverses with a bull bar: enter long beyond that reversal bar's high.
pseudocode: low[0] <= priorSessionClose + touchTicks * tick && close[0] > open[0] && (close[0] - open[0]) >= bodyFraction * (high[0] - low[0])
book_order_type: stop one tick beyond the pullback bar's high (long) / low (short)

complexity.reason: a fixed reference price (yesterday's close) compared against the current bar's low/high plus a single-bar trend-bar test

name: IsFirstBarOfSession
quote: Institutional traders have orders to fill before the day opens, and they want to fill them at the best possible price.
description: Shared primitive (redefined here per chapter convention, see also V17-01): the current bar is the first bar of the session, i.e. its session date differs from the prior bar's.
pseudocode: ctx.SessionDate(0) != ctx.SessionDate(1)

complexity.reason: requires a session/date-change accessor

name: TimeOfDayReversalWindow
quote: the trader needs to be aware that the market often reverses around 8:30 a.m. PST, and be prepared to take the trade.
description: Context filter: bars whose close time falls within a window around a known scheduled-report time (e.g. 8:30 a.m. exchange-adjusted) carry elevated odds of a trend start or reversal, regardless of whether it is still 'the opening range'.
pseudocode: ctx.Time(0) >= windowStart && ctx.Time(0) <= windowEnd

complexity.reason: a plain bar-close-time comparison, though the specific time is exchange/market-dependent (U.S. economic data releases at 8:30 a.m. ET/PST-quoted here)

notes: The underlying reason (scheduled economic reports) is data the engine does not have, but the clock-time pattern itself is directly decidable from the bar timestamp, close to the existing TimeWindow rule shape.

name: AvoidEntryNearSessionClose
quote: The day was over and there was not enough time left for the bears to make a profit, so they therefore chose to not short into the close.
description: Do not initiate a new intraday entry once the session clock is within X minutes of the close; there is not enough remaining time for a typical trade to reach a profit target.
pseudocode: ctx.Time(0) < (sessionCloseTime - minMinutesBeforeClose)

complexity.reason: a single comparison against the bar's close time; the book gives no exact minute threshold so one is invented

name: FirstHourExtremeFilter
quote: since the high or low of the day usually forms in the first hour and this was a possible high of the day.

name: FinalHourWithTrendEntry
quote: When the market is in a bull trend, look for buy setups in the final hour. Likewise, when the daily chart is in a bear trend, look for sell setups in the final hour
description: Intraday: when the daily-chart trend is up (proxy: today's session close so far above the session open, or prior daily closes rising), allow/take long entries only in the final hour of the session. Page 316 adds the bear form: 'a huge plunge in the final 30 minutes' on bear days.

name: OpenNearSessionExtreme
quote: Note how the open of the day was very close to the low of the day, which is a sign of strength, and trend from the open days that open within a few ticks of the low of the day often close within a few ticks of the high of the day.
description: The session's open still sits within a small distance of the session's running low (bull case) -- a sign this is a trend-from-the-open bull day likely to close near its high.
pseudocode: (sessionLowSoFar - open[0]) > -nearThreshold && (open[0] - sessionOpenPrice) == 0

complexity.reason: needs the session's opening price and its running low/high tracked as state

name: OpeningRangeHeight
quote: The opening range usually provides clues to how the day will unfold
description: Primitive: the opening range of the session is the highest high minus the lowest low of the first N bars of the session. Exposed as a local for the other TP4 candidates; as a standalone filter it is true once N bars of the session have printed.
pseudocode: barsIntoSession = count of bars since the first bar of this Date (0-based); if (barsIntoSession < openingBars) return false; orHigh = highest(high over the first openingBars bars of the session); orLow = lowest(low over the same bars); orHeight = orHigh - orLow; return true

complexity.reason: needs session-boundary detection from the Date series and a per-session persistent high/low

notes: Brooks defines the opening range loosely ('first 30 to 60 minutes', elsewhere 'first five to 10 bars'); 12 bars = one hour of 5-minute bars.

name: AverageDailyRange
quote: If the opening range is about half of the range of the recent days
description: Primitive: the average of the full-session high-low range over the last D completed sessions, computed on the intraday series by tracking each session's running high and low and rolling them at the Date change.
pseudocode: on Date change: push (sessionHigh - sessionLow) into dailyRanges, reset sessionHigh/sessionLow; adr = average(dailyRanges, dailyLookback); return dailyRanges.size() >= dailyLookback

complexity.reason: cross-bar state: a per-session high/low and a ring buffer of completed session ranges

notes: Brooks says 'recent days' without a count; 5 is a reading.

name: HalfOpeningRangeTrendingRangeDay
quote: If the opening range is about half of the range of the recent days, the breakout will often lead to a measured move and a trending trading range day.
description: Filter: the opening range is between a lower and an upper fraction of the average daily range (around one half), so a breakout is expected to travel about one opening-range height and then form a second range; entries in both directions are allowed afterwards.
pseudocode: orHeight >= lowFraction * adr && orHeight <= highFraction * adr

complexity.reason: composes two per-session state primitives

notes: Chapter 22 restates this as 'a third to half' and 'first hour or two', hence openingBars 24 here.

name: PatternRecognitionWindow
quote: you will find that you can see them potentially setting up in the first 30 to 60 minutes
description: Filter: the day-type classification (TP4-03/04/06) is only trusted once the session is at least M minutes old; before that, treat the day as undecided (both directions allowed, scalps only).
pseudocode: minutesSinceSessionOpen(Time) >= classifyAfterMinutes

name: OpeningRangeHeightVsAverageDailyRange
quote: The opening range is about a third to half the size of the range of recent days.
description: Primitive with state: track the current session's opening-range high/low over its first N bars, and the average of the last M completed sessions' full-day range (high-low). Exposes openingRangeHeight and avgDailyRange for later candidates.
pseudocode: newSession = Date(0) != Date(1); if (newSession) { if (haveOpeningRange) pushDailyRange(sessionHigh - sessionLow); sessionHigh = high[0]; sessionLow = low[0]; barsIntoSession = 0; openingRangeSet = false } else { barsIntoSession++; sessionHigh = max(sessionHigh, high[0]); sessionLow = min(sessionLow, low[0]) } if (!openingRangeSet && barsIntoSession == openingRangeBars) { openingRangeHigh = sessionHigh; openingRangeLow = sessionLow; openingRangeHeight = openingRangeHigh - openingRangeLow; openingRangeSet = true } avgDailyRange = average(lastNDailyRanges, dayLookback)

complexity.reason: needs session-boundary detection and a rolling multi-day range history built up from intraday bars, not a plain windowed average

notes: openingRangeBars must be tuned to the bar size in use; Brooks means roughly the first one to two hours.

name: SmallOpeningRangePredictsExpansion
quote: If the opening range is about a third to half of the size of the recent average daily range, then look for a breakout and an approximate doubling of the range of the day.
description: Filter: the session's opening-range height is at or below a fraction of the recent average daily range, which favors a breakout later in the session and roughly a doubling of the day's range. Enables the breakout and measured-move candidates below.
pseudocode: openingRangeSet && openingRangeHeight <= smallRangeFraction * avgDailyRange

name: LateSessionReversalAfterTrendingRangeDay

description: Filter/context: on a day already classified as a trending trading range day, a countertrend reversal attempt in the final N minutes of the session is a reliable setup (retracing at least the most recent trading range), unlike earlier in the day.
